passage: Rain had pushed Ishita's birthday party indoors, and twenty children were squeezed into one small living room. Maria stood behind her mother's legs, holding the gift. 'Say hello to Ishita, beta! Don't be shy!' an aunty said loudly. Maria pressed her face into the back of Mama's knee and went still. 'She'll come when she's ready,' Mama said, and sat on the sofa, letting Maria lean. Maria watched the block tower grow for a long time. Then she walked over, held out the gift and whispered, 'Happy birthday.' Ishita beamed. 'Want to build?' Maria nodded and knelt beside her.

qa.q: Why was the party indoors?
qa.a: Rain had pushed it indoors.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the aunty told her to say hello?
qa.a: She felt shy and overwhelmed, freezing with her face pressed into Mama's knee.

qa.q: What did Mama do that helped Maria join in?
qa.a: She didn't push; she sat down, let Maria lean and watch, and said she'd come when she was ready.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Maria whispers 'Happy birthday'?
qa.a: Ishita is pleased and welcoming, beaming and inviting Maria to build.

grounding: Shows a young child who hides behind a parent at a crowded party, freezes when pushed to say hello, and joins after watching.

passage: At the colony's Diwali get-together, Mohit held on to the back of Papa's kurta. When Mrs. Kapoor bent down and asked his name, he whispered it into Papa's sleeve. 'Go, play with the boys!' Dadi said, giving him a little push. Mohit went stiff and started to cry. Papa picked him up. 'Let's just watch for a bit.' From Papa's arms, Mohit watched Jomon and three others rolling marbles along chalk lines. Then he tapped Papa's shoulder. 'Down.' He crouched at the edge of the game. Jomon slid a blue marble toward him without a word.

qa.q: What were Jomon and the others doing?
qa.a: Rolling marbles along chalk lines.

qa.q: Why did Mohit go stiff and cry when Dadi pushed him?
qa.a: Being pushed made him frightened and more frozen, because he needs time before joining.

qa.q: What did Papa do differently from Dadi?
qa.a: He picked Mohit up and let him watch for a while, so Mohit could choose when to join.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Mohit crouching at the edge?
qa.a: Jomon seems friendly and easygoing, sliding a marble over without making a fuss.

grounding: Shows a young child who whispers answers, freezes when pushed to play, and joins only after being allowed to watch.

passage:
'Papa, do I have to say hello to everyone at the wedding?'
'Who told you that?'
'Masi. Last time.' Kishore pulled at his sherwani button. 'My tummy went hard.'
Vikas sat on the bed. 'You don't have to. You can stand with me and watch first.'
'And then?'
'Then, if you want, you can wave. Or show someone your car.'
At the wedding Kishore stood behind Vikas, watching the cousins race round the chairs. Then he tugged his hand. 'Papa. Can I show Guddu my car?'
'Go on.'
He went, slowly, holding the car out like a ticket.

qa.q: What did Kishore want to show Guddu?
qa.a: His car.

qa.q: What does Kishore's 'My tummy went hard' show?
qa.a: He felt nervous and scared when he was pushed to say hello to everyone.

qa.q: Why did Vikas's plan help?
qa.a: It let Kishore watch first and choose his own small step, like showing his car, instead of forcing hellos.

qa.q: How might Masi's 'say hello to everyone' have felt to Kishore?
qa.a: It made Kishore feel pressured and frozen, which is why he still remembered it with worry.

grounding: Shows a young child who wants to join in but needs time, and a parent who lets him watch first rather than pushing him to say hello.

passage:
Monday. At recess Tenzin stood by the wall with a tennis ball in his pocket, watching the football game. He practised the words in his head: Can I play? He didn't say them.
Wednesday. Rehana, who sat beside him in class, jogged over. 'We need a goalkeeper. Want to?' Tenzin nodded before he could think. He saved one shot and laughed too loudly, then worried all afternoon that he'd looked silly.
The next Monday. Tenzin walked up to the game himself. His heart thumped. 'Can I play?' 'Obviously,' said Rehana. 'Goal's yours.'

qa.q: What did Tenzin keep in his pocket?
qa.a: A tennis ball.

qa.q: What was Tenzin worried about on Wednesday afternoon?
qa.a: He felt anxious that laughing too loudly had made him look silly.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin ask to play by the next Monday?
qa.a: Rehana's friendly invitation gave him a safe first go, and that practice made asking for himself feel possible.

qa.q: Why might Rehana have invited Tenzin?
qa.a: Rehana may have noticed him watching by the wall and guessed he wanted to join but was waiting to be asked.

grounding: Shows a child who longs to join a game but waits to be invited, is helped by a peer's friendly bridge, and grows braver with practice.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage: Damini, you think you're the only one who waits at the edge? When your Sangeeta Mausi was ten, in Nashik, the girls played kho-kho every evening on the temple ground. I wanted to play so badly my feet itched. But I sat under the neem tree, pretending to read, waiting for someone to call me. I kept thinking, what if I run the wrong way, what if they laugh? A whole month of evenings. Then a girl called Kusum walked over and dropped her dupatta in my lap. 'Hold this for me, and then you're on my team.' I played badly that day. Nobody laughed. By Diwali I was the one calling the new girls in.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta sit while the girls played?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, pretending to read.

qa.q: What was young Sangeeta worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that she would run the wrong way and the girls would laugh.

qa.q: What turning point let Sangeeta join the game?
qa.a: Kusum walking over, handing her the dupatta and putting her on the team, a friendly bridge into the game.

qa.q: Why might Kusum have walked over?
qa.a: Kusum probably noticed Sangeeta watching every evening and guessed she wanted to play.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a child who longed to join a game but waited to be invited, until a peer offered a friendly bridge.

subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]
passage: Jaya had joined the school in November, halfway through the year, and on the first rainy day recess moved indoors. Four girls were playing carrom at the back table, laughing. Jaya wanted to play so much it ached. But all four seats were taken, and what would she even say? 'Can I have next game?' sounded pushy; 'I'm good at carrom' sounded like showing off. She sat at her desk sharpening a pencil that was already sharp. Irawati, striker in hand, looked up. 'You play?' Jaya's cheeks went hot. 'A little.' Irawati shifted her chair. 'Squeeze in, be my partner. I'm terrible at the red.' Jaya perched on the edge of the chair. By the end of recess she had pocketed the red twice, and said four whole sentences.

qa.q: What was Jaya doing while the others played?
qa.a: Sharpening a pencil that was already sharp.

qa.q: What was Jaya worried about before Irawati spoke?
qa.a: She was anxious that anything she said would sound pushy or like showing off.

qa.q: What made Irawati's invitation work so well?
qa.a: It was casual and made room without pressure, and asking Jaya to be her partner offered a friendly bridge into the game.

qa.q: What might Irawati have noticed about Jaya?
qa.a: Irawati may have noticed the new girl watching the game and guessed she wanted to join.

grounding: Shows a new child longing to join a game but holding back for fear of saying the wrong thing, until a peer makes room.

passage:
Friday
Everyone says I'm shy. Mummy says it when aunties visit: 'He's the shy one.' Dadi says it. Even my cousin says it. So I stay quiet, because that's what shy people do. Today in science Bhavna Ma'am asked why the ice melted faster in the steel bowl. I knew. My heart was going fast, but I put my hand up halfway, and she saw. I said it very softly. She didn't say, 'Oh, our shy boy spoke!' like Mrs. Iyer did last year. She said, 'That was a brave thing, putting your hand up. And a good answer.' I've been thinking about 'brave' all evening. Nobody has called me that before. Maybe I'm not the shy one. Maybe I'm someone who can do brave things.
Darshan

qa.q: What question did Bhavna Ma'am ask in science?
qa.a: Why the ice melted faster in the steel bowl.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on being called brave?
qa.a: He felt surprised and quietly proud, thinking about the word all evening.

qa.q: What did Bhavna Ma'am do differently from Mrs. Iyer?
qa.a: She avoided the 'shy' label and praised the brave step of raising his hand, so he felt capable rather than defective.

qa.q: What might the aunties think when Mummy says 'He's the shy one'?
qa.a: They probably accept it as a fact about Darshan, not realising the label is shaping how he sees himself.

grounding: Shows a child who has started to believe the 'shy' label everyone gives him, and a teacher who praises a small brave step instead.

passage: In the village near Karnal, everyone had decided Payal was shy. 'She won't talk,' her Dadi told visitors. 'Don't expect anything from her.' So Payal didn't talk. When her Chacha Akash came home from the city for Lohri, he noticed she stood behind the door whenever guests came. He didn't call her shy. On the second evening he handed her a ten-rupee note. 'Can you buy me some rewri from Ramlal's shop?' Payal's stomach flipped. She went, stood at the counter a long time, and finally said, 'Rewri, please.' When she came back, Akash Chacha grinned. 'You asked him yourself? That took guts.' That night, when guests came for the bonfire, Payal stood by the door again, but in front of it this time.

qa.q: What did Akash Chacha ask Payal to buy?
qa.a: Some rewri from Ramlal's shop.

qa.q: What did Payal feel when handed the note?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped; she felt nervous about speaking to the shopkeeper.

qa.q: How did Akash Chacha help without labelling Payal?
qa.a: He gave her a small brave task and praised her for it, so she saw herself as capable rather than 'shy'.

qa.q: How might Dadi's words to visitors affect Payal?
qa.a: Hearing 'She won't talk' again and again made Payal believe it, so she stayed silent.

grounding: Shows a child who has come to believe she is 'the shy one', and an adult who avoids the label and praises a small brave step.

passage: At Leila's school in Lisbon, the report cards had said the same thing for three years: 'Leila is very shy.' Leila had read them. Now, in class games, she stood at the back, because that's where the shy girl stood. Her new teacher, Senhor Paulo, never used the word. On Tuesday he noticed she had read a whole page aloud to her partner in pair reading, quietly but without stopping. At the end of the lesson he knelt by her desk. 'You read that whole page to Inês. That was a brave step.' Leila looked at her shoes, but her mouth twitched. On Thursday, when he asked for a volunteer to hand out books, her hand went up, just to her shoulder. He saw it. 'Leila, thank you.'

qa.q: What had the report cards said for three years?
qa.a: 'Leila is very shy.'

qa.q: What does Leila's mouth twitching suggest?
qa.a: She felt pleased and a little proud, even while looking at her shoes.

qa.q: Why did Senhor Paulo's praise work?
qa.a: He named a specific brave step instead of the label, so Leila felt capable and tried another small step on Thursday.

qa.q: How might Inês have experienced Leila's reading?
qa.a: Inês heard Leila read a whole page, and may have seen her as a steady partner rather than 'the shy girl'.

grounding: Shows a child who has come to see herself through the 'shy' label, and a teacher who avoids it and praises small brave steps.

passage: Kalyani, I heard you skipped the class trip again. Sit with me. When your Vidya Atthe was fifteen, in Mangaluru, I was so afraid of being laughed at that my world got smaller every month. I wouldn't answer in class, even when I knew. I rehearsed 'One masala dosa, please' for an hour before going to the canteen, then went hungry rather than say it. I missed my own cousin's engagement because I was sure everyone would stare. It wasn't just shyness; fear was running my days. Then Mrs. Pinto, my English teacher, kept me back after class. She didn't scold. She said, 'I think you're carrying something heavy. Shall we go to the counsellor together?' We went that same afternoon. It took a year of small steps. But I came back to my own life.

qa.q: What did Vidya rehearse before going to the canteen?
qa.a: 'One masala dosa, please.'

qa.q: What was young Vidya feeling that made her skip her cousin's engagement?
qa.a: She was afraid, sure that everyone would stare and judge her.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vidya get her life back?
qa.a: Mrs. Pinto noticing, speaking kindly and going with her to the counsellor that same afternoon, followed by a year of small steps.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Pinto have seen Vidya in class?
qa.a: Mrs. Pinto seems to have seen a student carrying something heavy, not a rude or lazy one, and cared enough to act.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager whose fear of embarrassment was intense enough to shrink her life, and the support that helped.

passage: The history presentation had been moved to tomorrow, and Naveen had been at his desk since six, whispering the same four sentences. By ten he had written them out fourteen times. 'I'll just be absent,' he told his sister Mahima when she brought him tea. She sat on his bed. 'That's the third thing this term. You skipped the quiz club and Farhan's birthday too.' He stared at the page. 'Everyone will see my voice shake. They'll talk about it for weeks.' 'That fear sounds huge,' Mahima said. 'Bigger than normal nerves. It's making your life smaller.' He didn't answer. 'So, tonight, say it once to me. Just once. Tomorrow, go. And this week we tell Amma and ask to see the school counsellor. You shouldn't fight this alone.' Naveen let out a long breath, and nodded.

qa.q: How many times had Naveen written out his sentences?
qa.a: Fourteen times.

qa.q: What was Naveen afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid everyone would see his voice shake and talk about it for weeks.

qa.q: What plan did Mahima suggest, and why does it go beyond tonight?
qa.a: Say it once to her, go tomorrow, and tell Amma and see the school counsellor this week, because the fear is shrinking his life and needs support.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel seeing Naveen at his desk at ten?
qa.a: Mahima was probably worried, having noticed a pattern of skipped events, and decided he needed more than a pep talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager who rehearses for hours and skips events out of intense fear of embarrassment, and a sister who recognises it calls for support.

passage: Samir noticed that Abhinav hadn't said a word in English class all term, even when Ms. Rego looked straight at him. He had missed the inter-house quiz, the Class 10 picnic, and Samir's own birthday dinner in Bandra, with a last-minute text: 'Sorry, headache.' On Friday, walking to the station, Samir finally asked. Abhinav kept his eyes on the pavement. 'I write out what I'll say before I say anything. Even to the canteen uncle. Sometimes for an hour. If I get one word wrong, I feel like everyone will remember it forever.' 'That sounds exhausting,' Samir said. 'It is.' 'Would you tell your mum? Or the counsellor? I'll come with you if you want.' Abhinav was quiet for two stations. Then: 'Mum. Tonight.' At nine he texted Samir: 'Told her. Seeing the counsellor Monday.'

qa.q: What did Abhinav text before Samir's birthday dinner?
qa.a: 'Sorry, headache.'

qa.q: What is Abhinav afraid will happen if he gets one word wrong?
qa.a: He is afraid everyone will remember it forever, a strong fear of embarrassment.

qa.q: Why was Samir's offer to come along helpful?
qa.a: It made asking for help less lonely, and led Abhinav to tell his mum and book the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt about the missed birthday dinner before Friday?
qa.a: Samir may have felt hurt or puzzled, until he understood the fear behind it.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose intense fear of being judged makes him rehearse every sentence and skip events, and a friend who helps him seek support.

passage: Every time Pablo had to speak in class at his London school, his body went off like an alarm: heart racing, face burning red, mind wiped white. In October he stood up to present on volcanoes and forgot his second sentence. He replayed it every night for a week. So when the next presentation came, he stayed home with a stomach ache. The relief was huge, for about a day. Then the fear of the next one grew bigger. His form tutor sent him to Ms. Nkechi Obi, the school counsellor. She didn't tell him to just be brave. Together they made a ladder: read one line to her; then to two friends; then ask one question in class. 'Your body is trying to protect you,' she said. 'We'll teach it, slowly.' In December Pablo asked one question in geography. His face went red. He asked it anyway.

qa.q: What was Pablo's October presentation about?
qa.a: Volcanoes.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel after staying home from the next presentation?
qa.a: He felt huge relief for about a day, then the fear of the next one grew bigger.

qa.q: Why is Ms. Obi's ladder better than staying home?
qa.a: Small, gentle steps with support teach his body it can cope, while avoiding only made the fear larger.

qa.q: How does Ms. Obi see Pablo's racing heart and blushing?
qa.a: She sees them as his body trying to protect him, something to retrain slowly, not a weakness.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose body reacts strongly before speaking, who finds avoidance brings brief relief but bigger fear, and who improves with gentle, supported steps.

passage: At basketball practice, Coach Alka told Gargi she would give the team talk before the zonal match. Gargi's heart began to race right there on the court. By evening she had a plan: be sick on match day. The thought felt like relief. Coach Alka caught her at the water cooler. 'You went red as a tomato when I said it. Talk to me.' Gargi blurted it out: the blushing, the blank mind, the way she replayed every word for days. 'And if I skip it, I'm fine.' 'For a day,' said Coach Alka. 'Then the next talk feels twice as big. How about this: tomorrow, one sentence to me. Thursday, to the three starters. Saturday, the whole team, with notes.' Gargi swallowed. 'And if my face goes red?' 'Then it goes red, and you keep talking.'

qa.q: What was Gargi supposed to give before the zonal match?
qa.a: The team talk.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel when she planned to be sick on match day?
qa.a: She felt relief, as if skipping would make the fear go away.

qa.q: What steps did Coach Alka suggest?
qa.a: One sentence to the coach tomorrow, then to the three starters on Thursday, then the whole team on Saturday with notes: gentle, supported exposure.

qa.q: How did Coach Alka read Gargi's red face?
qa.a: Coach Alka noticed a player struggling and chose to talk and help, rather than let her quietly avoid the talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose racing heart, blushing and blank mind push her to avoid speaking, and a coach who offers gentle, step-by-step practice instead.

passage:
Dear Vidya Didi,
You asked me to write when I tried the first step, so here it is. You know what happens to me: before I talk in front of people, my heart pounds, my face goes hot, and my head empties like a tipped bucket. Afterwards I replay every word like a crime.
For two years I just avoided things. Every time I skipped, I felt better that night and worse the next month.
This week, as we planned with the school counsellor, I did step one: I read out the attendance list in chemistry. My voice wobbled on the third name. My face was on fire. Then it was over, nobody said anything, and Rafiq asked me for a pen like normal.
I replayed it only twice. Step two is next Tuesday. I'm scared. I'm going anyway.
Akash

qa.q: What did Akash read out in chemistry?
qa.a: The attendance list.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about step two?
qa.a: Akash is scared but determined to go anyway.

qa.q: Why is reading the attendance list a good first step?
qa.a: It is a small, manageable step planned with the counsellor, showing Akash that the feared moment passes and nobody reacts.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vidya would probably feel proud and encouraged, seeing Akash take a first step after two years of avoiding.

grounding: Shows a teenager who describes the racing heart and blank mind before speaking, sees that avoidance made fear larger, and starts gentle steps with help.

passage:
'Quiz club's meeting at four. Want to come?'
Madhav shook his head. 'Too many people.'
'Okay. No pressure.' Chinmay packed his bag. 'If you ever want to just sit at the back, I'll save a seat.'
'You always say that.'
'Because it's always true.'
Madhav almost smiled. 'If they ask me something, can you answer for me? Just the first time?'
'If you want me to. Just tell me.'
The next week Madhav came, sat at the back, and whispered one answer: the capital of Peru. Chinmay nudged him. 'You said a thing. In a room.'
'Don't make it a big deal.'
'A small deal. A good small deal.'
Walking home, Chinmay said carefully, 'You've been skipping lunch too, lately. If it's getting in the way, the counsellor's actually nice. I could come.' Madhav was quiet. 'Maybe. Thanks.'

qa.q: What did Madhav answer at the quiz club?
qa.a: The capital of Peru.

qa.q: What does Madhav's request that Chinmay answer for him show?
qa.a: He felt anxious about speaking in a group but wanted to come, needing someone to cover for him the first time.

qa.q: What makes Chinmay's support wise?
qa.a: He invites without pressure, speaks for Madhav only when asked, celebrates a small step, and gently suggests the counsellor since the fear is affecting lunch too.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel about Chinmay's 'small deal'?
qa.a: Madhav probably felt embarrassed but pleased, glad the step was noticed without fuss.

grounding: Shows a friend who invites without pressure, speaks for a quiet friend when asked, celebrates a small step and gently suggests a counsellor.

passage: When Siddharth joined our class in Class 9, he didn't speak for a month. I'm Damini, and I sat next to him in chemistry. I didn't push. I'd say, 'We're getting chaat after school, come if you want,' and leave it there. Some days he came and just ate, listening. Once, during group work, he slid me a note: 'Can you present our part? I'll do the slides.' So I did, and I said clearly, 'Siddharth made these slides.' He went pink but didn't look unhappy. Then in December he told me he'd stopped going to his cousin's house because even family dinners made his chest tight, and he hadn't slept properly in weeks. That's when I said, as gently as I could, 'I think a counsellor could help with that. Want me to walk you there?' He went the next Monday.

qa.q: What did Siddharth write in the note?
qa.a: 'Can you present our part? I'll do the slides.'

qa.q: What might Siddharth have felt when Damini credited his slides?
qa.a: He likely felt embarrassed but pleased, going pink without looking unhappy.

qa.q: When did Damini suggest a counsellor, and why then?
qa.a: When Siddharth said the fear was stopping family dinners and sleep, because that meant it was affecting normal life and needed professional help.

qa.q: What might Damini's no-pressure invitations have meant to Siddharth?
qa.a: They let him join on his own terms, sometimes just listening, so he felt included without being forced to perform.

grounding: Shows a friend who invites without pressure, speaks for a quiet classmate when asked, gives him credit, and suggests a counsellor when fear stops normal life.

passage:
House parent's note, junior hostel, week 6
I want to record something good. Lakshmi, who arrived in June, still finds the dining hall hard; she eats fast, head down, and leaves. Omkar, from her class, has quietly started sitting at the end of her table with a book. He doesn't make her talk. At yesterday's talent evening I heard him ask her, 'Do you want to be on the list, or just watch?' She said watch. He said, 'Cool,' and sat with her at the back. When she clapped along to one song, he gave her a thumbs-up, nothing more. Later he came to me and said Lakshmi had told him she's been skipping classes because walking in late feels impossible. I spoke with her that evening, and she has a meeting with the school counsellor tomorrow.
R. Thomas, house parent

qa.q: What does Omkar bring when he sits at Lakshmi's table?
qa.a: A book.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have gone to the house parent, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He was probably worried about Lakshmi once she said she was skipping classes, and knew the fear was stopping normal life, so an adult needed to know.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's habits make him a good support for Lakshmi?
qa.a: He sits nearby without making her talk, offers a choice instead of pushing her to perform, and marks a small step with just a thumbs-up.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about 'Do you want to be on the list, or just watch?'
qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt relieved and respected, free to choose without being pushed to perform.

grounding: Shows, in a house parent's note, a friend who keeps a quiet classmate company without pressure, celebrates small steps and brings in adult help when fear stops normal life.

passage: At the international students' welcome party in Rotterdam, Bao lasted forty minutes. He said hello to three people, smiled a lot, and slipped out before the dancing. He wasn't upset. He cycled home through the drizzle, made noodles and felt fine. On Thursday Noa, a classmate, cornered him kindly. 'You should come out more. Join the debate society, work on your shyness.' Bao felt a flicker of irritation. 'I don't really suffer from it,' he said. 'I like a few people a lot.' It was true. Every Sunday he cooked pho with two friends from his course, and they talked for hours about their families and what they wanted from life. Noa thought about that. 'Can I come on Sunday?' Bao smiled. 'Bring bread.'

qa.q: How long did Bao stay at the welcome party?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Bao feel when Noa suggested he work on his shyness?
qa.a: He felt a flicker of irritation, because being quiet doesn't make him suffer.

qa.q: What does Bao's Sunday cooking show about his style?
qa.a: His reserved temperament suits small, deep friendships where he talks for hours, so it isn't a problem to fix.

qa.q: How does Noa's view change by the end?
qa.a: Noa moves from wanting to fix Bao's shyness to wanting to join the Sunday cooking.

grounding: Shows a young adult who is quiet with strangers but content, finding depth in a few friendships, and irritated at being told to fix it.

passage: The warden of the engineering hostel, Mahima Ma'am, kept a list of students who never came to events. Vaibhav's name was on it: no freshers' night, no Holi party, no cricket league. In February she knocked on his door, a little worried. Inside, Vaibhav and two friends were bent over a chessboard, a flask of tea between them. 'Everything all right, Vaibhav? You never come to anything.' He stood up, polite and quiet. 'I'm fine, Ma'am. Big crowds aren't my thing. These two are.' One friend laughed. 'He's the reason I haven't dropped out. He listens.' Mahima Ma'am looked at them, the board, the notebook of chess games in his neat hand. 'All right,' she said. 'Just checking.' That evening she crossed his name off the list.

qa.q: What were Vaibhav and his friends doing?
qa.a: Playing chess, with a flask of tea between them.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav feel about missing hostel events?
qa.a: He feels calm and content, simply preferring a few close friends to big crowds.

qa.q: Was Mahima Ma'am right to check on Vaibhav? Why?
qa.a: Yes; checking was caring, and she listened and accepted that his quietness was temperament, not a problem.

qa.q: What does the friend's remark reveal about Vaibhav?
qa.a: That Vaibhav's depth as a listener matters a great deal to the friend, who credits him with not dropping out.

grounding: Shows a reserved young adult who skips big events but is content, with deep, valued friendships, and a warden who accepts it is not a problem.

passage:
Dear Divyansh,
You asked in your last message whether I'm 'still hiding' in Pune. I laughed, but I want to answer properly.
I'm not hiding. I'm still quiet with new people; at the department dinner last week I said about ten words, and most of them were 'pass the raita'. But I don't lie awake about it, and I don't feel I'm missing anything. I have three friends here I'd trust with anything. We cook on Sundays and argue about films till midnight.
When you and Ma try to fix my shyness, it makes me a bit cross, honestly. It's just how I'm built. It's also why I remember your exam dates and you remember nobody's.
Come and visit in March. You'll see.
Dhruv

qa.q: What did Dhruv mostly say at the department dinner?
qa.a: 'Pass the raita.'

qa.q: How does Dhruv feel when Divyansh and Ma try to fix the shyness?
qa.a: Dhruv feels a bit cross, since the quietness isn't causing any suffering.

qa.q: What would be a more helpful response from Divyansh?

passage: In her first semester at the Delhi college, Kashish had a timetable full of seminars and attended almost none. She would sit outside the seminar room, hear the voices, and walk back to the hostel. She ate in her room so no one would watch her eat alone. When the professor split the class into project groups, she emailed to ask if she could work by herself. At night she told herself she was pathetic. Her roommate Lakshmi noticed the unopened textbooks, the empty noodle cups, the way Kashish flinched at a knock. One evening Lakshmi sat on the edge of her bed. 'You don't have to tell me anything. But the student counselling centre is on the second floor of the library, and they're kind. I went last year. I'll walk you there tomorrow if you want.' Kashish stared at the ceiling. Then she said, 'Okay.'

qa.q: Where is the student counselling centre?
qa.a: On the second floor of the library.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling at night?
qa.a: She felt lonely and ashamed, telling herself she was pathetic.

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi's offer well judged?
qa.a: She didn't demand an explanation, shared that she had gone herself, and offered to walk Kashish there, making early help easier to reach.

qa.q: What had Lakshmi noticed about Kashish?
qa.a: The unopened textbooks, the empty noodle cups and the way Kashish flinched at a knock.

grounding: Shows a student who avoids seminars, meals and group work because being watched feels unbearable, and a roommate who points her early to a counsellor.

passage: By the middle of second year I had built a very small life. I'm Urmila. I stopped going to seminars because I couldn't bear everyone turning when I spoke. I ate lunch alone on the back stairs of the library. When Mohit asked me to join his project group, I said I preferred working alone. I didn't. I was lonely in a way that sat on my chest like a weight, and every night I listed my failures. What changed was a poster outside the canteen: 'Feeling stuck? Talk to us.' I walked past it eleven times. The twelfth time, I went in. The counsellor didn't tell me to just be confident. We started tiny: one seminar, sitting by the door. I wish I'd gone in first year. It would have saved me a lot of lonely lunches.

qa.q: What did the poster outside the canteen say?
qa.a: 'Feeling stuck? Talk to us.'

qa.q: How did Urmila feel during second year?
qa.a: Urmila felt lonely, like a weight on the chest, and self-critical, listing failures every night.

qa.a: Mohit probably took it at face value, not knowing Urmila wanted to join but was afraid of being watched.

grounding: Shows a student whose fear of being watched led to skipped seminars, lonely lunches and self-criticism, and the difference a counsellor made.

passage: The train to Madurai was two hours late, and the platform was packed. Kavitha was hopping between the yellow lines when a boy running past knocked her down.
